Feature stores in real-time ML pipelines promise consistent, low-latency feature access, but the central question is this: when upstream data sources update asynchronously and at different cadences, how do you reason about the joint staleness distribution of a feature vector at inference time, and how does that distribution diverge from the joint distribution seen during training? The key concepts are feature freshness windows (each feature has a tolerable staleness budget), computation graph topology (some features are derived from others, creating staleness cascades), and the training-serving skew that emerges not from code bugs but from temporal misalignment — the training data saw features computed at time T, but serving sees features computed at T minus some heterogeneous lag. A beginner worries about single-feature staleness ("is this feature too old?") and misses that the correlational structure between features changes under asynchronous staleness — two features that were highly correlated in training become decorrelated at serving time when one updates at 1-minute cadence and another at 15-minute cadence, and the model, never having seen this decorrelation pattern, extrapolates into a regime it was never trained on. What experts lose sleep over is that this skew is not uniform across the input space: high-traffic entities get fresher features because their pipelines flush more frequently, while long-tail entities accumulate staleness, which means model performance degrades precisely where data is already sparse — and standard aggregate metrics like AUC obscure this completely because high-traffic entities dominate the evaluation set.

The mechanism is a staleness envelope problem: F_c is only recomputed when its computation job triggers, which is scheduled on its own cadence — not on the cadence of either parent. If F_a updates every 1 minute and F_b every 15 minutes, but the job that computes F_c runs every 20 minutes, then at the moment of serving F_c may have been computed 19 minutes ago using an F_a value that was itself already 1 minute stale and an F_b value that was 14 minutes stale — yet the recorded timestamp on F_c reflects only when F_c's job ran, not the effective data age of its inputs. This timestamp laundering is the core trap: feature stores like Feast and Tecton stamp features with their write time, not with the minimum freshness of their lineage, so downstream consumers and monitoring systems see F_c as "19 minutes old" when its effective staleness — defined as wall-clock time minus the timestamp of the oldest data that influenced it — is 19 + 14 = 33 minutes. Across a multi-hop graph this compounds multiplicatively in the worst case: if F_d depends on F_c and F_e (itself derived), and F_d's job runs every 30 minutes, the effective staleness envelope is the sum of all scheduling lags plus the maximum parent staleness at each hop, and on a 3-hop graph with aggressive scheduling misalignment you can reach effective staleness an order of magnitude beyond any single feature's nominal freshness SLA. Uber's Michelangelo documentation (circa 2017) implicitly describes this when noting that "feature freshness" in their system was monitored per-feature rather than per-lineage, meaning SLA violations in derived features were systematically underreported. The compounding is worst at join nodes where two high-cardinality streaming features merge, because backpressure or reprocessing in one parent branch causes the join to hold stale data from the other parent while waiting — a pattern described in the Flink community as "watermark skew" causing downstream operators to buffer unboundedly or emit prematurely stale records.

The minimum sufficient statistic you must propagate is a staleness provenance vector: for each feature write, store (1) the wall-clock write timestamp of the current node, and (2) the minimum source event time across all raw data sources that influenced this computation — what you might call the "lineage floor." Everything else — intermediate node timestamps, job execution times, parent write times — can be reconstructed if needed but is not required for effective staleness calculation at serving time, because effective staleness = serving wall-clock time minus lineage floor. The lineage floor must be propagated as a scalar (or a small fixed-size vector if you want per-source-system granularity), and at each computation node the job simply takes min(lineage_floor of all inputs) before writing — this makes propagation O(fan-in) per node and O(depth) across the graph, both of which are small constants in practice for typical ML feature graphs with depth < 10 and fan-in < 20. The storage overhead is modest: one additional int64 timestamp per feature row, which for a Feast-style feature store backed by Redis adds roughly 8 bytes per entity-feature pair — negligible against the feature value payload itself, which is typically 4–32 bytes per scalar feature. The latency cost is more subtle: at write time, the computation job must wait for all parent lineage floors to be readable before it can write its own, which introduces a coordination dependency that did not exist in the fire-and-forget asynchronous model; in systems like Tecton that use Spark for batch feature computation, this requires joining the lineage metadata table alongside the feature join, adding one extra shuffle per hop that can inflate job latency by 10–30% depending on partition skew. Google's Sibyl system and the broader literature on data provenance (Cheney et al., "Provenance in Databases," 2009) distinguish between why-provenance (which source records contributed) and when-provenance (their timestamps), and for staleness tracking you only need when-provenance, which is why the scalar lineage floor suffices — full why-provenance would be computationally intractable at feature store scale. The practical trap is that lineage floor propagation breaks silently when any node in the graph fails to instrument correctly — a single legacy feature computation job that writes without a lineage floor causes all downstream nodes to fall back to write-time stamping, so you need schema enforcement (e.g., making lineage floor a non-nullable column) and monitoring for nodes emitting lineage floor equal to their write time, which is the telltale signature of an uninstrumented node.

The serving layer has four concrete response options: (1) serve with stale features and log a staleness flag, (2) impute the stale feature (with mean, last-known-good, or a fallback model), (3) block and recompute on-demand, or (4) reject the request and return a default score or abstain. Option 1 is the most common default and its hidden failure mode is that the staleness flag is almost never fed back into the model, so the model applies full confidence to a degraded input — worse, if staleness correlates with the prediction target (e.g., a user's activity features go stale precisely because they churned), the model systematically mispredicts the highest-value cases, and the staleness flag in logs creates an illusion of observability without actually mitigating the error. Option 2 sounds safe but introduces a distributional shift of its own: mean imputation collapses variance and destroys the signal in tail values, and last-known-good imputation silently reverts to an arbitrarily old value that may be further from the true current value than the stale feature was — Uber's ML platform team noted in internal postmortems (referenced obliquely in their 2019 Michelangelo paper) that imputation during feature outages caused prediction distributions to shift enough to trigger downstream business logic anomalies. Option 3 (on-demand recomputation) appears correct but its failure mode is latency amplification under exactly the conditions when staleness is most likely — infrastructure stress events cause both feature staleness and high serving latency simultaneously, so blocking recomputation adds P99 tail latency precisely when the system is already degraded, potentially cascading into timeout storms. Option 4 (abstain or default score) is the most honest response but is operationally dangerous because default scores must be calibrated against the abstention rate — if 15% of requests receive a default score of 0.5 and your downstream system treats 0.5 as "uncertain, take conservative action," the effective policy change can have large business impact that is invisible in model metrics because abstentions are excluded from evaluation.

To detect this empirically at serving time, you can run a staleness-stratified score distribution test: partition served requests by effective staleness decile and compute the KL divergence or Wasserstein distance between the score distributions of fresh versus stale cohorts — if staleness is random noise, these distributions should be similar; if staleness is target-correlated, the stale cohort will show score compression toward the mean and a depleted tail, which is detectable with sample sizes in the thousands within minutes. A second detection strategy exploits feature variance collapse: under random staleness, feature value variance is preserved in expectation, but under target-correlated staleness the features of high-risk entities revert toward population mean (because their recent divergent behavior is not captured), so monitoring per-feature variance stratified by staleness tier — without any labels — reveals the signal; this is essentially a covariate shift detection method, related to the approach in Rabanser et al. This alone is necessary but not sufficient, because if you only log when the model is called, you inherit the selection bias of the existing system — entities that were already being scored, with whatever staleness distribution the current infrastructure produces — and you never see the counterfactual of what features would have looked like for entities that were not scored due to abstention or system failures. The second structural change is therefore staleness-stratified deliberate sampling: during data collection, explicitly oversample entities whose features are in staleness violation, score them anyway (even if the production system would abstain), and record both the stale feature vector and — when the label eventually arrives — the outcome, so the training set contains examples of the model operating under staleness conditions proportional to or exceeding what serving will encounter. Third, you must instrument staleness as an explicit input feature in training data, not merely as metadata: the effective lineage staleness of each feature (or a summary statistic like max staleness across the vector) becomes a first-class model input, so the model learns a staleness-conditional prediction function P(Y|X, S) rather than conflating fresh and stale regimes into a single P(Y|X) — this is structurally similar to what Johansson et al. describe in the causal inference literature as "including the treatment assignment mechanism as a covariate" to avoid confounding. The second failure mode is staleness magnitude overfitting: in training data, staleness values occupy a specific empirical range determined by your infrastructure's historical performance, and the model learns thresholds and interactions within that range; if infrastructure improves (reducing staleness) or degrades (increasing staleness beyond training distribution), the model's staleness-conditional predictions extrapolate into regimes it has never seen, potentially inverting the learned relationship — a gradient boosted tree, for instance, will clip predictions at the boundary of the staleness values seen in training leaves, producing flat, uninformative outputs for out-of-range staleness. Third, interaction term explosion: staleness is not independent of feature values — a stale activity count of 0 means something different than a fresh activity count of 0, and the model must learn this interaction for every feature whose staleness is included, which multiplies the effective feature space and requires substantially more data to fit reliably; in practice, trees learn these interactions implicitly but neural networks require explicit staleness-feature product terms or attention mechanisms to capture them, and without sufficient data the model collapses to ignoring staleness or ignoring the feature value, neither of which is correct. The minimum intervention on training data is to include a sufficiently rich proxy for Z as a covariate — concretely, this means adding features that capture the latent disengagement state independently of the staleness-inducing mechanism, such as server-side event counts (which are recorded regardless of feature pipeline health) or external signals like support ticket activity; if Z is fully observed, conditioning on it blocks the backdoor and the residual S→prediction error relationship is identified from observational data alone, following the backdoor adjustment formula in Pearl's do-calculus.
